By default, _TRANSPORT contains [[T0]], the screen, label and menu conversion program installed in your [[T1]] directory or folder.

To specify a program other than [[T4]] to transport your screens, labels and reports, store the program's name in _TRANSPORT. If your conversion program is in a directory other than the current default directory, include the path with the program name.

If you rename [[T5]] or move it to another directory, store the new filename and/or its directory in _TRANSPORT.

You can also specify a conversion program in your [[T6]] configuration file by including the following line:

 _TRANSPORT = file name

Add-Ins are code files (usually .prg or .scx) that provide an easy way for you to adjust the Coverage Profiler. The cov_standard subclass of the coverage engine, which comprises the User Interface of [[T0]], shows only a small part of what you can do with the engine. The engine analyzes the coverage log; cov_standard just displays the results in one of many ways you could want to see them.

You could create a different subclass of cov_engine with a very different display. For example, your subclass might display a dialog that runs queries against the coverage statistics gathered by the engine. The display options might provide a view of the marked code for a filtered set of log entries, or only a graph of the profiling results.

You might not want to subclass cov_engine to create a new interface from scratch because the cov_engine class provides an easier process. You can add functionality to cov_standard, or any cov_engine subclass, using Add-Ins. Cov_standard exposes this feature through a button in the main dialog of Coverage Profiler. When you run an Add-In on an instance of cov_standard such as Coverage Profiler, the Add-In can manipulate the capabilities of cov_engine, the coverage tables, as well as cov_standard. Add-Ins might also add new dialogs and features to the cov_standard visual interface.
You can write Add-Ins to enhance the standard interface or you can subclass cov_standard to create your own wholly new interface.

The following list includes features you might want to provide through Add-Ins:
 - Add a visible feature to the main dialog.
- Add a dialog into the coverage engine formset (reference limitation below on how to make sure your dialog shows up in the right place).
- Display a separate dialog that accesses a Coverage engine feature (reference limitation below on how to make sure your dialog shows up in the right place).
- Provide a querying interface that uses the Source table and presents a list of all lines that meet your criteria, and filters or orders the results. Note You can use the Adjust... methods ([[T0]], [[T1]], and [[T2]]) of the Engine to add fields to the Source and Target tables when the engine creates them, and use these fields in your Add-Ins.
- Add file names to the IgnoredFiles cursor, to eliminate those files from analysis. This can save analysis time.
- Use the special Init hook for Add-Ins.
- Register Add-Ins for retrieval and easy access to a list of Add-Ins. The modal dialog class cov_AddInDialog in the standard coverage engine subclass, presents previously registered dialogs in a drop-down list. When you set the coverage engine [[T3]]-In option [[T4]], the full path name of successfully run Add-Ins are added to the Windows Registry so you can easily run these Add-Ins again. The Standard [[T5]] class also allows you to set this property in the Coverage Profiler Options dialog box . The Coverage Engine object maintains a list of all registered Add-Ins in the [[T6]] property.
- Use the final [[T7]] field information, callstack, to design your own interface or your own view of the coverage log.
textos.d0a7df7a-701b-400e-877b-a9c89b355cb4#153:
When you write Add-Ins, consider the following information:
 - You can use any of the supported file types as Add-Ins. The supported file types are .qpr, .qpx, .mpr, .mpx, .app, .exe, .scx, fxp, .prg and .procedures (if the procedures are already available in an open procedure library).
- The Coverage Engine formset has an "invisible" toolbar. If your Add-In is nonvisual you can use this toolbar to contain it. If your Add-In is a visual control, the standard subclass main dialog .Cov_tools member container is probably the most convenient place to put it. This allows the position and size of the toolbar to be automatically synchronized with the rest of the dialog when it is resized.
- All the engine methods that use the Source and Target tables take optional arguments that allow you to point these methods at the appropriate aliases while you're working with them. You can also change the current [[T0]] and [[T1]] property contents to match the pair of cursors in which you are interested. This allows you to compare multiple Coverage log runs to each other within the same interface.
- Limitations: Add-Ins must accept one parameter (the Coverage engine passes a reference to itself). An Add-In must be one of the permitted file types, listed above. Procedures you use as Add-Ins should be available in a currently loaded procedure library (see [[T2]] Command ) in Help. The Engine does not use the [[T3]] FileName syntax, and it does not call procedures or .prg files as functions and [[T4]] their values. It does not use the [[T5]] or [[T6]] keywords on the [[T7]] command; you can either manage the reference yourself, or allow the Engine to scope a form for you by making your form a member of the Engine formset. If you run an Add-In at startup, you must use a reference because the public _oCoverage variable is not yet available. At other times, you can use the public variable reference within your own code, if you prefer. When you write an Add-In as a form, if you create the form as ShowWindow = 1 and run Coverage in its own frame, your Add-In forms should display in the Coverage frame. If you use .RunAddIn from the Command window, make sure the coverage frame is the active [[T8]] frame before you instantiate your forms.

You can subclass either the coverage engine or its standard subclass. The following list describes the structure of the [[T0]] project source file set.

| File | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [[T1]] | A "wrapper" for the coverage object, which instantiates the object. |
| [[T2]] [[T3]] | All classes for the engine and its standard subclass. |
| [[T4]] [[T5]] | Shortcut menu. |
| [[T6]] [[T7]] | Default mechanism to deliver project-level results. |
| [[T8]] | Header file for all Coverage code, incorporating the following elements: *— Coverage character constants for log and parsing: #[[T9]].H *— Coverage localized strings (can use some log and parsing constants): #[[T10]].H *— Coverage common dialog component constants: #[[T11]].H *— Coverage specs & requirements: #[[T12]].H *— Coverage registry object constants: #[[T13]].H *— Coverage tune-able options: #[[T14]].H |

The [[T15]] project source file set also includes various .ico .bmp, and .msk files.

Use the file [[T16]] (containing appropriate comments and explanations) to become familiar with options available to you without rewriting code.

Because Add-In use is governed by the coverage engine base class, any other coverage subclass you create can use Add-Ins in the same manner as the standard subclass.

The coverage engine subclass instantiated by the default [[T0]] does not augment the coverage engine [[T1]] method in any way. It does, however, invoke a modal dialog box to allow the user to pick an Add-In before it invokes the coverage engine [[T2]] method. The modal dialog box receives a reference to the Coverage object and sets the coverage engine [[T3]] property.

If you write your own coverage engine subclass, ensure that your subclass can use the same modal dialog class (cov_AddInDialog) to handle Add-Ins as the standard Coverage application; the dialog box does not rely on any features of the standard subclass.

You can call a different modal dialog box, set the [[T4]] file name directly in the [[T5]] property, or override the contents of the [[T6]] property by passing the name of the Add-In file you wish to run to the [[T7]] method.

However you access an Add-In to run in your subclass, you can investigate the list of Add-Ins registered to [[T8]] by checking the file names in the coverage engine [[T9]] property.

For details on the Properties, Events, and Methods of the coverage engine, see Coverage Engine Object in Help.

Creates a set of radio buttons or picture radio buttons.

[[C0]]

row, column

 Row and column are numeric expressions with values of 0 or greater that determine where the first button in a set of radio buttons appears.

 The first row is number 0 in the main [[T0]] window or a user-defined window. Rows are numbered from top to bottom. In [[T1]] for Windows, row 0 is the row immediately under the [[T2]] system menu bar. In [[T3]] for Macintosh, row 0 is the row immediately under the [[T4]] title bar. In [[T5]] for [[T6]]-[[T7]], row 0 is the row the [[T8]] system menu bar occupies. See [[T9]] for information about manipulating the system menu bar so you can place output on row 0 in [[T10]] for [[T11]]-[[T12]].

 The first column is number 0 in the main [[T13]] window or a user-defined window. Columns are numbered from left to right.

 When the first button in a set of radio buttons is directed to a user-defined window, the row and column coordinates are relative to the user-defined window, not the main [[T14]] window.

 In [[T15]] for Windows and [[T16]] for Macintosh, a position in the main [[T17]] window or in a user-defined window is determined by the font of the main [[T18]] window or the user-defined window. Most fonts can be displayed in a wide variety of sizes, and some are proportionally spaced. A row corresponds to the height of the current font; a column corresponds to the average width of a letter in the current font.

In [[T0]] for Windows and [[T1]] for Macintosh, you can position the first button in a set of radio buttons in a window with decimal fractions for row and column coordinates. In [[T2]] for [[T3]]-[[T4]], decimal fractions used for row and column coordinates are rounded to the nearest integer value.

[[T5]] memvar | field

 When you choose a radio button, your choice is stored to the memory variable or array element memvar or to the field field. memvar or field must be of numeric or character type.

 If memvar or field is of numeric type, a number corresponding to your radio button choice is stored to the memory variable, array element or field specified with memvar or field. For example, if you create three radio buttons and choose the second button, 2 is stored. If memvar or field is of character type, the prompt of the radio button you choose is stored to the memory variable, array element or field specified with memvar or field.

 Initial Radio Button Selection

 When a set of radio buttons appears, the value of memvar or field determines which radio button (if any) is initially selected.

If memvar or field is numeric, the radio button corresponding to the numeric value is initially selected. For example, if memvar or field is 1, the first radio button you define is initially selected. If memvar or field doesn't correspond to any of the buttons (the value is less than 1 or greater than the number of radio buttons) no button is initially selected.

 If memvar or field is of character type, a case-sensitive comparison is made between memvar or field and each radio button prompt. When the comparison is made, all special characters and any leading or trailing spaces are removed from the button prompts. If a match is found, the matching button is initially selected. If a match can't be found, no button is initially selected.

[[T0]] [[T1]] | [[T2]] [[T3]]

 When creating a set of radio buttons, you must include the [[T4]] clause, the [[T5]] clause or both. There is no advantage to any of the three methods. The [[T6]] or [[T7]] clause contains the radio button specification code *R and the text for the individual radio button prompts.

The [[T0]] character expression [[T1]] must begin with *R. To create the radio button prompts, include a space after *R followed by a list of the prompts separated by semicolons. One button is created for each prompt. For example, the following [[T2]] clause creates three radio buttons with the prompts None, Single and Double:

 ... [[T3]] '*R None;Single;Double' ...

 The [[T4]] character expression [[T5]] uses the same syntax as the [[T6]] expression except the [[T7]] expression must begin with @ followed by *R. For example, the following [[T8]] clause creates three radio buttons with the prompts None, Single and Double:

 ... [[T9]] '@*R None;Single;Double' ...

 You can also include both the [[T10]] and [[T11]] clauses to create radio buttons. If both are included, the [[T12]] character expression [[T13]] must contain *R to create the radio buttons and can also include a space and some radio button prompts. The [[T14]] character expression [[T15]] can include prompts to create additional radio buttons.

 The following examples illustrate the various forms of syntax you can use to create a set of radio buttons. The radio buttons begin in the second row and second column. Three radio buttons are created with the prompts None, Single and Double. A number corresponding to the button chosen is stored to the memory variable [[T16]].

 [[T17]] clause only:

[[T0]] 1 [[T1]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T2]] mchoice [[T3]] '*R None;Single;Double'

 [[T4]] 1 [[T5]] mchoice

 [[T6]] '*R None;Single;Double' [[T7]] mfunc

 @ 2,2 [[T8]] mchoice [[T9]] mfunc

 [[T10]] clause only:

 [[T11]] 1 [[T12]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T13]] mchoice [[T14]] '@*R None;Single;Double'

 [[T15]] and [[T16]] clause:

 [[T17]] 1 [[T18]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T19]] mchoice [[T20]] '*R' [[T21]] ' None;Single;Double'

 [[T22]] 1 [[T23]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T24]] mchoice [[T25]] '*R None;Single' [[T26]] ';Double'

 [[T27]]

Radio Buttons with Picture Prompts

 In [[T28]] for Windows and [[T29]] for Macintosh, the prompt for a radio button can also be the name of a picture file. In [[T30]] for Macintosh, you can use a picture file of [[T31]] type or a .[[T32]] bitmap file.

 When a radio button uses a picture file for a prompt, the radio button mimics the behavior of a radio button with a text prompt. For example, the picture file appears but the radio button isn't displayed. Like choosing a radio button, choosing the picture prompt stores the radio button's value to memvar or field.

To use a picture file in a radio button, add B to the radio button specification code. The [[T0]] and [[T1]] clause specification codes that create a radio button are *R and @*R, respectively. To create a radio button with picture prompts, use the codes *[[T2]] and @*[[T3]], followed by a space and the picture filename. If the picture file is not located in the default directory or folder, include the path to picture file with the picture filename.

 -------------------------------

 Note - The pictures aren't clipped, reduced or enlarged to fit the radio button. Use the [[T4]] clause to adjust the size of the radio buttons to accommodate the pictures.

 -------------------------------

 If you omit the extension for the picture file, [[T5]] for Macintosh first looks for a picture file with the name you specified and a .[[T6]] extension. If a picture file with a .[[T7]] extension and the name you specified isn't found, [[T8]] for Macintosh then looks for a file with the name you specified and a .[[T9]] extension. If a picture file with a .[[T10]] extension and the name you specified isn't found, [[T11]] for Macintosh then looks for a picture file with the name you specified without an extension.

Picture Masks and Radio Buttons

In [[T0]] for Windows and [[T1]] for Macintosh, a picture radio button has three states: up, down and disabled. [[T2]] automatically controls the appearance a picture radio button when it is in each of these three states, but you can override the default appearance by using a picture mask.

 A mask is used to control the transparent areas of a picture radio button. By default, the white areas are transparent. If a mask is present, the white areas of the mask, not the picture file, are transparent.

 A mask is a monochrome picture file. In [[T3]] for Windows, a mask is a .[[T4]] with an .[[T5]] extension. In [[T6]] for Macintosh, a mask can be a .[[T7]] with an .[[T8]] extension or a [[T9]] type file with a .[[T10]] extension. The mask must have the same base name as the picture file and the appropriate extension. [[T11]] automatically looks for a mask for a picture file in the same directory or folder where the picture file is located.

 In most cases, a mask isn't necessary. If you don't need anything in your picture to appear white or your picture file has a white background, the picture radio button will appear as desired in the up, down and disabled states.

When a picture radio button has a mask and is in the up or down state, any white areas in the picture file appear transparent, allowing the color of the button face to show through. However, you can maintain the white color of certain areas. Suppose that you have a picture file with a dog on a white background; the dog has white eyes and the button face is red. You want the background of the button to appear red but you want the dog's eyes to be white, not red. Make a mask that is the same size as the picture file but includes only two colors, black and white. Leave the background of the mask white but make the dog - including his eyes- completely black. When the button appears, the background is red to match the button face but the dog's eyes are white.

 When a picture radio button is disabled, any white areas in the picture file appear transparent so the color of the button face shows through. Any non-white areas appear dark gray. If the button has a mask, all white areas in the mask are transparent so the color of the button face shows through, and all black areas appear dark gray.

[[T0]] and [[T1]] Options N, T, H, V, 2 and 3

 Additional options can be combined with the *R specification code to modify the behavior (N and T) and appearance (H, V, 2 and 3) of radio buttons.

The 2 (two-dimensional) and 3 (three-dimensional) specification codes are only available in [[T0]] for Macintosh.

 Option Description

 N Does not terminate the [[T1]] when a radio button is chosen. This is the default behavior.

 T Terminates the [[T2]] when a radio button is chosen.

 H Positions the radio buttons in a horizontal row.

 V Positions the radio buttons in a vertical column. This is the default orientation.

 2 Creates flat (two-dimensional) radio buttons identical to radio buttons in Macintosh dialogs. This is the default radio button type in [[T3]] for Macintosh.

 3 Creates three-dimensional radio buttons identical to radio buttons in [[T4]] for Macintosh dialogs.

 You can combine the T or N options with the H or V and 2 or 3 options. For example, the following clause creates a vertical row of radio buttons and doesn't cause the [[T5]] to terminate when a button is chosen:

 ... [[T6]] '*[[T7]] ... '

 In [[T8]] for Macintosh, the following clause creates a vertical row of two-dimensional radio buttons and doesn't cause the [[T9]] to terminate when a button is chosen:

 ... [[T10]] '*[[T11]] ... '

Radio Buttons with Special Features

You can assign a hot key to a radio button or disable a radio button. To assign these special features to a radio button, you must include special characters when defining the prompt. The special characters are removed when the prompt is stored to memvar or field.

Hot Keys

 In [[T0]] for [[T1]]-[[T2]], a hot key is a highlighted letter in a radio button prompt that you can type to immediately choose the radio button. Pressing the hot key selects the radio button and chooses it. To assign a hot key, place a backslash and a less-than sign (\<) before the desired character of the radio button prompt.

 A hot key doesn't choose the radio button if the current object is a [[T3]] field, a text-editing region, a popup or a list.

 If the current object is an @ ... [[T4]] input field or a text-editing region, pressing the hot key enters the character in the field or the text-editing region. If the current object is a pop-up or a list, pressing the hot key selects the first option in the popup or list whose prompt begins with the hot key character.

 In [[T5]] for Windows, a hot key is an underlined letter in the radio button prompt that you can type to immediately choose the radio button. If the current object is an @ ... [[T6]] input field, a text-editing region, a popup or a list and [[T7]] is set to [[T8]], you can press the Alt key and the hot key to choose the radio button.

In [[T0]] for Macintosh, the [[T1]] setting determines if hot keys are underlined. If [[T2]] is set to [[T3]] or [[T4]], hot keys are underlined. If [[T5]] is set to [[T6]], hot keys are not underlined but are still available.

 The following example creates three radio buttons with the prompts None, Single and Double and assigns the hot keys N to None, S to Single and D to Double:

 [[T7]] 1 [[T8]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T9]] mchoice [[T10]] '*R' [[T11]] '\<None;\<Single;\<Double'

 [[T12]]

Disabled Radio Buttons

 You can disable a radio button so it can't be selected or chosen. Disabled buttons are shown in disabled colors. To disable a single radio button, place two backslashes (\\) before the button's prompt. To disable a set of radio buttons, use [[T13]], which is discussed later in this section.

 The radio button with the prompt Single is disabled in this example:

 [[T14]] 1 [[T15]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T16]] mchoice [[T17]] '*R' [[T18]] 'None;\\Single;Double'

 [[T19]] [[T20]] [, [[T21]]]

 The character expression [[T22]] is the name of the font, and the numeric expression [[T23]] is the font size. For example, the following clause can be used to display the radio button prompts in 16-point Courier font:

 [[T24]] 'Courier', 16

 If you include the [[T25]] clause but omit the font size [[T26]], a 10-point font is used.

In [[T0]] for Windows, if the font you specify is not available, a font with similar font characteristics is substituted.

 In [[T1]] for Macintosh, if the font you specify is not available, the Chicago font is used.

 In [[T2]] for [[T3]]-[[T4]], the [[T5]] clause is ignored.

 If the [[T6]] clause is omitted and the radio buttons are placed in the main [[T7]] window, the main [[T8]] window font is used. If the [[T9]] clause is omitted and the radio buttons are placed in a user-defined window, the user-defined window font is used.

[[T10]] [[T11]]

 In [[T12]] for Windows and [[T13]] for Macintosh, include the [[T14]] clause to specify a font style for the radio button prompts. If the font style you specify is not available, a font style with similar characteristics is substituted.

 The font style is specified with [[T15]]. If the [[T16]] clause is omitted, the normal font style is used.

 Character Font Style

 --------- ----------

 B Bold

 - Strikeout*

 * The Condense and Extend styles are only available in [[T17]] for Macintosh. The Strikeout style is only available in [[T18]] for Windows.

 You can include more than one character to specify a combination of font styles. For example, the following clause specifies Bold Italic:

 [[T19]] '[[T20]]'

The [[T0]] clause is ignored in [[T1]] for [[T2]]-[[T3]].

[[T4]] expr

 When you choose a radio button, your choice is saved in the memory variable, array element or field you specify. If you specify a memory variable that doesn't exist, it is automatically created and initialized if you include the [[T5]] clause. However, an array element isn't created if you specify an array element in a [[T6]] clause. The [[T7]] clause is ignored if the memory variable already exists or you specify a field.

 If the [[T8]] clause isn't included and memvar doesn't exist, the error message "Variable not found" appears.

 The [[T9]] expression expr determines the type of memory variable created and its initial value. expr must be of numeric or character type. Here are examples of [[T10]] clauses for radio buttons:

 @ 2,2 [[T11]] mchoice [[T12]] '*R' + ;

 'None;Single;Double' [[T13]] 'Single'

 [[T14]]

 @ 2,2 [[T15]] mchoice [[T16]] '*R None;Single;Double' ;

 [[T17]] 2

 [[T18]] [[T19]], [[T20]] [, [[T21]]]

 The size [[T22]] clause specifies the height in rows of the radio buttons. In [[T23]] for [[T24]]-[[T25]], a radio button is always one line high, so the numeric expression [[T26]] is ignored.

 By default, the width of each individual button is determined by the length of the radio button prompt text. [[T27]] specifies the width (in columns) of each radio button.

By default, no rows are placed between vertical buttons and a single column is placed between horizontal buttons. The spacing between radio buttons in rows is specified with [[T0]].

 In [[T1]] for Windows and [[T2]] for Macintosh, the radio button font determines the size of the editing region. The radio button font is specified with the [[T3]] clause. If the [[T4]] clause is omitted, the radio buttons use the font of the parent window (the main [[T5]] window or a user-defined window).

 This example demonstrates how the [[T6]] clause control's the button spacing:

 [[T7]]

 @ 2,2 [[T8]] mchoice1 [[T9]] '*R'+ '\<None;\<Single;\<Double' ;

 [[T10]] 'None' [[T11]] 1, 12, 1

 @ 2,16 [[T12]] mchoice2 [[T13]] '*R'+ '\<None;\<Single;\<Double' ;

 [[T14]] 'None' [[T15]] 1, 12, 3

 [[T16]] | [[T17]]

 Radio buttons are by default enabled when [[T18]] or [[T19]] is issued. You can prevent a set of radio buttons from being selected when [[T20]] or [[T21]] is issued by including [[T22]].

 Disabled radio buttons cannot be selected and are displayed in the disabled colors. To disable individual radio buttons instead of an entire set, see "Disabled Radio Buttons" earlier in this section. Use [[T23]] to enable a set of disabled radio buttons.

[[T24]] [[T25]]

The [[T0]] clause character expression [[T1]] appears when a radio button is selected. In [[T2]] for [[T3]]-[[T4]] the message is by default centered on the last line of the main [[T5]] window. The message location can be changed with [[T6]].

 In [[T7]] for Windows and [[T8]] for Macintosh, the message is placed in the graphics-based status bar. If the graphics-based status bar has been turned off with [[T9]], the message is placed on the last line of the main [[T10]] window.

[[T11]] [[T12]] | [[T13]]

 You can include an optional [[T14]] expression [[T15]] or [[T16]] that is evaluated when a radio button is chosen. That is, [[T17]] isn't evaluated when you select (move to) a radio button, but when you actually choose the radio button by pressing Enter, Spacebar or clicking on the radio button.

 Typically, [[T18]] or [[T19]] is a user-defined function ([[T20]]). With a user-defined function ([[T21]]) you can select, enable or disable other objects, open a Browse window, open another data-entry screen or move to a new record. [[T22]] can be included in the user-defined function to terminate the [[T23]].

 [[T24]]

 When a logical value is returned to the [[T25]] clause, the logical value is ignored and the radio buttons remain the active control. However, you can specify a [[T26]] that returns a logical value to the [[T27]] clause and activates another object.

 [[T28]]

A [[T0]] clause that includes a numeric expression is used to specify which object is activated after a radio button is chosen. Objects are @ ... [[T1]] input fields, check boxes, lists, popups, spinners, text-editing regions and each individual button in a set of push, radio and invisible buttons.

 The expression [[T2]] has one of three effects:

  When [[T3]] = 0, the chosen radio button remains the active button.

  When [[T4]] is positive, [[T5]] indicates the number of objects to advance. For example, when the last radio button in a set of radio buttons is selected and [[T6]] returns 1, the next object is activated. If [[T7]] is greater than the number of remaining objects, the [[T8]] is terminated (unless [[T9]] is issued to activate the objects).

  When [[T10]] is negative, [[T11]] indicates the number of objects to move back. For example, when the first radio button in a set of radio buttons is selected and [[T12]] returns -1, the previous object is activated. If [[T13]] moves back past the first object, the [[T14]] is terminated (unless [[T15]] is issued to activate the objects).

[[T16]] [[T17]]

The [[T0]] clause allows or prohibits selection of a set of radio buttons based on the logical value of [[T1]], which must evaluate to a logical true ([[T2]]) before the radio buttons can be selected. If [[T3]] evaluates to a logical false ([[T4]]), the radio buttons cannot be selected and are skipped over if placed between other objects.

[[T5]] [[T6]] | [[T7]] color pair list

 If you do not include a [[T8]] clause, radio button colors are determined by the color scheme for the main [[T9]] window; if radio buttons are placed in a user-defined window, the window's color scheme determines the radio button colors.

 The colors of radio buttons can be specified by including the number of an existing color scheme in the [[T10]] clause or a set of color pairs in the [[T11]] clause.

 A color scheme is a set of 10 predefined color pairs. The color pairs in a color scheme can be changed with [[T12]]. In [[T13]] for [[T14]]-[[T15]] the color pairs in a color scheme can also be changed in the Color Picker.

 A color pair is a set of two letters separated by a forward slash. The first letter specifies the foreground color and the second letter specifies the background color.

 For example, this color pair specifies a red foreground on a white background:

 R/W

 For a list of colors and their corresponding color letters, see [[T16]] Overview or Color Table by Color Pair.

A color pair can also be specified with a set of six [[T0]] (Red Green Blue) color values separated by commas. The first three color values specify the foreground color and the second three color values specify the background color. The color values can range from 0 through 255.

 The R/W color pair in the example above can also be specified with this [[T1]] color pair:

 [[T2]](255,0,0,255,255,255)

 The following table lists the color pairs and what each color pair in the list controls.

 Color Pair Radio Button

 Number Attribute

 ---------- ------------

 5 Message

 6 Selected radio prompt

 7 Hot keys

 9 Enabled radio prompt

 10 Disabled radio prompt

 This example shows how to override one color scheme with another predefined color scheme:

 [[T3]] 1 [[T4]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T5]] mchoice [[T6]] '*R None;Single;Double';

 [[T7]] 4

 [[T8]]

 The following example creates None, Single and Double radio buttons with the hot keys N for None and S for Single. In addition, the buttons have the following color characteristics:

  The selected button is shown with a bright white prompt on a blue background (W+/B).

  Hot key characters are shown in red on a blue background (R/B).

  Enabled buttons are shown with a yellow prompt on a blue background ([[T9]]+/B).

  Disabled buttons are shown with a white prompt on a blue background (W/B).

When you skip a color pair, you must include a comma where the color pair is omitted.

 Here are the commands:

 [[T0]] 1 [[T1]] mchoice

 @ 2,2 [[T2]] mchoice [[T3]] '*R \<None;\<Single;\\Double';

 [[T4]] ,,,,,W+/B,R/B,,[[T5]]+/B,W/B

 [[T6]]

This variation of @ ... [[T0]] creates a set of radio buttons. As their name suggests, radio buttons are similar to the buttons of a car radio - choosing a button makes your choice current and releases your previous choice. A bullet next to a radio button indicates that it is the current choice.

If you use the Screen Builder to create your data-entry screens, you might not have to use this command at all. The Screen Builder automatically generates the commands that create radio buttons and picture radio buttons.

The string of text to the right of each button is called a prompt. The text of the prompt is specified with the [[T1]] or [[T2]] clause. Issue [[T3]] or [[T4]] to activate the buttons.

You can create picture radio buttons in [[T5]] for Windows and [[T6]] for Macintosh. Pictures replace the radio button prompts.
